_about: Why each class and relation exists, the question it answers, and who confirmed it.

Product.alternatives: A specific software-product class with releases and environments baked in; rejected because the user chose a generic vocabulary reused per project.
Product.question: Why does this product exist, and what is it? (A1)
Product.why: The root the whole vocabulary hangs off. Generic on purpose: one vocabulary every project starts from, a product being whatever the project sets out to build.

Role.alternatives: Role plus Person: rejected, no question needs a named individual's decisions traced. Stakeholder as one class: rejected, two people would populate it differently.
Role.question: Who owns it and who decides? (A4)
Role.why: Ownership questions are answered better by a role than a person, because roles are stable while people move; the holder is an attribute with history by supersession.

Persona.alternatives: Separate AntiPersona class: rejected, nothing points at it so it stays thin. Audience as a text attribute of Product: rejected, D1 and D2 lose their anchor.
Persona.question: Who is it for, and who is it not for? (A2)
Persona.why: Journeys, requirements and value propositions need something to point at, and the excluded audience must be a dated first-class fact, not a footnote.

ValueProposition.alternatives: Separate Problem class: rejected, no question traverses from problem to several propositions. Attributes on Product: rejected, nothing could trace to a purpose.
ValueProposition.question: Why does it exist, and what is the value proposition in one sentence? Which requirement serves which purpose? (A1, A3, D2)
ValueProposition.why: It is the traceability anchor: requirements, journeys and criteria trace to it, so an orphan requirement (failure F3) becomes a rule violation instead of folklore.

SuccessCriterion.alternatives: List attribute on ValueProposition: rejected, no history, no owner, which is exactly F4. Measurement class for observed readings: deferred until a question asks for readings.
SuccessCriterion.question: How do we know the product succeeded? (B2, failure F4)
SuccessCriterion.why: A target that changes needs history and an owner, and a product with none must be flaggable; an attribute list gives neither.

Requirement.alternatives: Folding requirements into Feature: rejected, a need and the capability that satisfies it have different owners and dates.
Requirement.question: What must the product do? What is in scope for the next release? (B3, B1)
Requirement.why: The unit a builder agent works from and a release scopes; it carries priority and kind, traces to a value proposition, and is what decisions are about.

Scenario.alternatives: UseCase class: rejected for now, a use case is a functional Requirement with its flow. Workflow class: rejected, a workflow is a UserJourney whose persona is a role.
Scenario.question: What exactly must this do in this situation, and how do we test it? (G5; Gate 3 review)
Scenario.why: A scenario is the concrete path tests and acceptance run on, with its own preconditions and expected result; it must be pointable from a test and a requirement.

Release.alternatives: Requirement.scope attribute: rejected, nothing to be in scope of, B1 and C3 unanswerable. A Scope node per release: rejected, the edges already carry it.
Release.question: What is in and out of scope for the next release, and what was the scope as of a past date? (B1, C3)
Release.why: Scope has to be scope OF something dated; edges to a release carry validFrom and validTo, so the boundary at any past date is readable.

Decision.alternatives: Decision as a status on the thing decided: rejected, no reason and no history.
Decision.question: What did we decide about X, when, and why? (C1, failure F1)
Decision.why: A decision has a date, a reason, evidence and a role that made it; a status field has none of those, and an agent needs to see a settled decision before reopening it.

OpenQuestion.alternatives: Decisions with state = open: rejected, populated differently. Hotspot class: deferred until the method runs gates on contested areas.
OpenQuestion.question: What is still open or unresolved? (C2)
OpenQuestion.why: An open question is raised before any reason or evidence exists and is later resolved by a decision; keeping it separate lets an agent list what is open before building.

owned_by.alternatives: A closed list of classes per side: rejected, two ontologies extending the same base could not both add to it.
owned_by.question: Who is accountable for this?
owned_by.why: Ownership is asked of products, requirements, releases and whatever an extension adds; one relation to a role answers it everywhere. One relation with an open side rather than a closed list of classes, so independent ontologies that extend this one compose without redeclaring it; the engine refuses two siblings widening the same relation.

decided_by.question: Whose call was it?
decided_by.why: A decision without the deciding role cannot be revisited with the right person.

offers.question: Which promises does the product make?
offers.why: The product-level entry to the traceability spine; a product usually makes more than one promise.

intended_for.alternatives: A closed list of classes per side: rejected, two ontologies extending the same base could not both add to it.
intended_for.question: Who is this for, and who is it not for?
intended_for.why: The audience is a fact about a promise, a journey or a report, and the excluded audience must be statable the same way. One relation with an open side rather than a closed list of classes, so independent ontologies that extend this one compose without redeclaring it; the engine refuses two siblings widening the same relation.

serves.alternatives: A closed list of classes per side: rejected, two ontologies extending the same base could not both add to it.
serves.question: Which requirement or journey serves which purpose? (D2)
serves.why: This is the edge the orphan-requirement policy runs on; without it F3 cannot be detected. One relation with an open side rather than a closed list of classes, so independent ontologies that extend this one compose without redeclaring it; the engine refuses two siblings widening the same relation.

measures.question: How do we know it succeeded?
measures.why: Ties a metric and a target to what it judges, so a promise with no criterion can be flagged. in_scope_of.question: What is in scope for the next release? (B1)
in_scope_of.why: Kept separate from excluded_from so absence of an edge means unknown, not out of scope. excluded_from.why: An explicit exclusion is a fact a builder must see; silence would be read as permission. about.question: What did we decide about X? (C1)
about.why: One wide relation rather than one per subject class, so a decision about anything is found the same way. resolves.why: Closing a question by a dated decision keeps the question and its answer connected.

blocks.why: Turns an open question into a release-level fact a gate can check; risks reach a release through threatens, so they were removed from this relation in the duplicate audit.
